title: The four risks a construction lender prices
summary: A construction lender worries about four things: will the building get built, will it fill, will its income cover the debt, and can the bank get out if it does not. A loan is approved when all four are visibly closed.
body:
Every construction lender is pricing four risks at once: completion, lease-up, cash flow and exit. Mr Shabazz, your whole package should be organised as the evidence that closes each of these four, in that order.

In plain English

Lending against a finished, rented building is relatively simple: the income is visible and the asset exists. Lending against a building that does not exist yet is harder, because the bank is betting that a series of future events will go right. Construction lenders have reduced that bet to four questions. If any one of them is left open, the loan is either declined, shrunk or priced higher.

The professional framing: the four risks

1. Completion risk

The fear: a half-built building that is worth less than the money spent on it. Half a building has almost no market. What closes it: a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum-price construction contract with a capable contractor, an independent quantity surveyor's or cost consultant's budget, a realistic contingency, approvals and permits in hand, and often a completion guarantee from the sponsor. Banks fear cost overruns more than low rents, because an overrun can stop the job entirely.

2. Lease-up or sales risk

The fear: a finished building that sits empty. What closes it: a market study, rent comparisons from similar buildings, signed pre-leases or pre-sales with deposits, or an agreement with an experienced operator. Signed income evidence outweighs any report.

3. Cash-flow risk

The fear: income that does not cover the loan payments once the building is running. What closes it: a debt service coverage ratio at or above the bank's minimum, tested under stress, such as lower rent, higher vacancy or higher interest rates. Week 3 shows how this is calculated.

4. Exit or recovery risk

The fear: a default that leaves the bank holding an asset it cannot sell or cannot legally take. What closes it: clean registered title, a realistic appraisal, insurable construction, and security documents that are enforceable in the courts where the land sits.

The professional framing: sequence matters

The four risks arrive in time order. Completion risk dominates during the build. Lease-up risk dominates at practical completion. Cash-flow risk dominates once the building is stabilised. Exit risk sits underneath all three. A good lender asks which risk is largest at each stage, and so should you when deciding where to spend money on mitigation. Money spent closing completion risk early is usually the most valuable, because a stalled job damages every later stage.

The professional framing: how the bank prices what stays open

A risk you cannot fully close does not always kill the loan. It usually changes the terms. An open completion risk shows up as a lower loan-to-cost ratio, a larger contingency requirement or a sponsor overrun guarantee. An open lease-up risk shows up as a requirement to pre-lease a minimum share of space before the first draw, or a larger interest reserve to carry the building while it fills. An open cash-flow risk shows up as a smaller loan sized to a higher coverage ratio. An open exit risk usually cannot be priced at all, because a bank that cannot take or sell its security has no second way out. Read each condition in a lender's offer as the price of a specific risk you left open, and ask whether closing that risk yourself would be cheaper than accepting the condition.

A worked example

A hypothetical borrower asks for a US$3,000,000 loan on a US$4,500,000 building. Here is what closes each risk, and what it costs.

  1. Completion. The borrower converts a cost-plus arrangement into a guaranteed-maximum-price contract. The contractor adds US$90,000 to its price for taking the overrun risk, which is 2 percent of cost. In exchange, the bank no longer has to assume an open-ended overrun.
  2. Lease-up. The borrower signs two pre-leases covering 40 percent of the floor area at the forecast rent. Cost: about US$30,000 of leasing commission and fit-out concessions.
  3. Cash flow. With 40 percent pre-leased, the forecast at 75 percent occupancy still covers debt service 1.21 times, so the bank's 1.20 times minimum holds even if the remaining space leases slowly.
  4. Exit. Title is transferred into the borrowing company and registered; the bank's appraiser values the completed building at US$5,200,000. The loan is 58 percent of that value.

Roughly US$120,000 of spending, under 3 percent of cost, has converted four open questions into four closed ones. That is usually the cheapest money in the whole project.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is completion, and it is the one first-time developers underestimate. A building that runs out of money at 70 percent complete is not 70 percent as valuable as a finished one. It is often worth less than the land, because a buyer must price in demolition or the cost of fixing unknown work. This is why lenders insist on cost certainty, contingency and, often, a guarantee that someone will fund the overrun.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner asks the bank to fund the uncertainty. "Once you lend, I will sign the contractor, find tenants and finish the approvals." Banks lend against risk you have already removed; they do not lend so that you can remove it. Do the de-risking work, at your own cost and with your own equity, before the formal application.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, open your risks section with four headings: completion, lease-up, cash flow, exit. Under each, list the evidence you have, the evidence you lack, and the cost of getting it. Then rank the gaps by how much each would move a lender, and close the cheapest high-value gap first. Your construction training gives you an advantage on completion risk: a credible schedule, a reviewed scope and a contract with clear change-order rules speak directly to a lender's largest fear. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer for the contract form, licensed cost consultant or quantity surveyor for the budget.
checklist: Completion: fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum contract, independent budget, contingency, permits.
Lease-up: market study, rent comparisons, signed pre-leases or pre-sales.
Cash flow: coverage at or above the minimum under stress.
Exit: clean registered title, realistic appraisal, insurable asset, enforceable security.
The risks dominate in time order; completion usually matters most.
Banks lend against risk already removed, not to fund its removal.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A borrower has a strong market study but a cost-plus contract with a contractor who has never built at this scale. Which risk will the bank focus on, and what two changes would most help?
selftest.a: Completion risk. A cost-plus contract leaves overruns open, and an unproven contractor raises the chance of a stalled job. The two changes: convert to a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum-price contract with an experienced contractor (or add a stronger contractor or construction manager), and commission an independent cost consultant's budget with a realistic contingency; a sponsor completion or overrun guarantee may also be requested.

apply: For a hypothetical project, write the four risk headings and list one piece of evidence you have and one you lack under each.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Parts 3 and 4. The four construction risks, the order of what tips a yes, loan types and the construction-loan lifecycle are commercial lending practice, not law, and vary by lender [unverified — confirm with each lender]. Contract forms such as fixed-price and guaranteed-maximum-price agreements should be reviewed by a construction lawyer.

title: What actually tips a lender to yes
summary: Beyond closing the four risks, a handful of factors decide whether a lender commits: your cash in first, cost certainty, income certainty, clean legal position, coverage headroom, sponsor depth, simplicity and relationship value. A first-time developer offsets a missing track record by hiring one.
body:
Lenders do not weigh every strength equally; your own cash spent first, fixed costs and signed income usually count for more than anything else. Mr Shabazz, a first-time developer cannot buy a track record but can rent one, by hiring a team that has done it before.

In plain English

Two projects can both close the four construction risks on paper and still get different answers. The difference is in how convincingly, and in a set of softer factors that make a credit committee comfortable. Experienced developers know which factors carry the most weight and spend their effort there.

The professional framing: what tips a yes, in rough order of weight

The ordering below reflects common senior-lender practice; individual lenders weight things differently [unverified — confirm with each lender].

  1. Your cash in first and at risk. Equity spent before the bank's first dollar, and ranking behind the bank. It proves conviction and absorbs early losses.
  2. Certainty of cost. An independent budget and a contract with a fixed price or guaranteed maximum.
  3. Certainty of income. Signed leases, pre-sales with deposits or a credible operator agreement.
  4. Clean legal position. Title registered in the borrower's name, approvals in writing, the borrowing company incorporated, and clear authority to borrow.
  5. Coverage headroom. A coverage ratio comfortably above the minimum, so a 10 percent rent miss does not break the covenant.
  6. Sponsor depth. Your liquidity and net worth outside the project, and the professionals you have hired where you lack experience.
  7. Simplicity. One borrower, one asset, one currency, a plain structure. Every extra entity, investor class or currency adds questions.
  8. Relationship value. Deposits, operating accounts and future business that make the loan more profitable for the bank.

The professional framing: the first-time developer offset

A committee asks of a new sponsor: who on this team has done this before? You answer by hiring experienced people into the roles where failure is most expensive.

  • Experienced general contractor, on a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum contract, with completed projects of similar size.
  • Independent cost consultant or quantity surveyor, who prepares the budget and later certifies each draw.
  • Owner's representative or development manager, who has delivered similar buildings and manages the process on your behalf.
  • Professional property manager, who signs a management proposal before completion and lends credibility to the operating forecast.
  • Experienced lawyers and accountants, whose names a committee recognises.

Banks underwrite the team, not only the principal. Put each person's name, role and relevant completed projects in the package.

The professional framing: what the team page must show

A list of names is not enough. For each hired professional, a committee wants three things: projects of similar type and size actually completed, the specific role they played on those projects, and the contractual basis on which they are working for you now. A contractor who built warehouses is weak evidence for an apartment building. A development manager engaged on a vague hourly basis is weaker evidence than one with a signed scope, a defined fee and responsibility for the schedule. References the bank can call, and lenders who have financed those people before, are the strongest evidence of all. Where a team member is still being selected, say so and state the selection criteria and timeline, rather than leaving the role blank or implying it is filled.

A worked example

A hypothetical first-time sponsor has a US$2,000,000 project. The bank initially offers 55 percent of cost, US$1,100,000, citing inexperience. Here is how she moves it.

  1. She hires a development manager with five completed buildings for a fee of US$60,000, 3 percent of cost, added to the budget.
  2. She signs a guaranteed-maximum-price contract with a contractor that has built eight similar buildings.
  3. She shows US$500,000 of liquid assets held outside the project, enough to fund a 20 percent overrun on the construction contract.
  4. She moves her business operating account and payroll to the bank.

The bank revises its offer to 65 percent of cost, US$1,300,000. The extra US$200,000 of loan reduces her equity requirement by the same amount. The development manager's fee cost US$60,000 and, with the other changes, released US$200,000 of equity. That is the economics of renting a track record.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is complexity creeping in. Each extra investor, holding company, currency or side arrangement adds a question for the committee and a document for the lawyers. A structure that is elegant for tax or ownership can be unattractive to a lender if it obscures who owns what, who is liable, and who gets paid first. Design the structure with the lender's simplicity test in mind, and take tax and legal advice on any trade-off.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to compensate for inexperience with optimism: larger rent forecasts, faster lease-up, a smaller contingency. To a committee, an inexperienced sponsor with an aggressive forecast is doubly risky. Do the opposite. The less track record you have, the more conservative your assumptions should be, and the more experienced your hired team.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, run your package against the eight factors in order and mark each as strong, adequate or weak. Fix from the top: more equity in first and firmer cost certainty usually move a lender more than anything lower on the list. Then write a team page that answers "who has done this before" with names and completed projects. Keep the structure as simple as your advisers allow. Professional sign-off required: lawyer and tax adviser for any entity or investor structure.
checklist: Your own cash, spent first and ranking behind the bank, carries the most weight.
Cost certainty and income certainty come next.
Clean legal position: registered title, written approvals, incorporated borrower, authority to borrow.
Coverage headroom so a 10 percent rent miss does not break the covenant.
Simplicity: one borrower, one asset, one currency.
A first-time sponsor rents a track record: contractor, cost consultant, development manager, property manager.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A first-time sponsor's package has a 5 percent contingency, a 12-month lease-up assumption in a market where comparable buildings took 20 months, and no development manager. What will a committee conclude, and what would you change?
selftest.a: It will conclude the sponsor is inexperienced and optimistic, which compounds the risk. Change: raise the contingency to a level an independent cost consultant supports, extend lease-up to match comparable evidence and show coverage still holds, and hire a development manager with completed projects so the team answers the experience question.

apply: List the people a first-time sponsor would need to hire to answer 'who has done this before', and the one credential a committee would want to see for each.

title: The types of loan you will meet
summary: A development usually uses a construction loan during the build, then a term mortgage once the building earns income. Bridge loans, construction-to-permanent facilities and corporate overdrafts each have a narrower job.
body:
A building is financed in stages: a construction loan pays for the build, and a term or permanent loan replaces it once the building earns rent. Mr Shabazz, choosing the wrong type of facility for a stage is one of the quietest ways a project gets into trouble.

In plain English

Different loans are built for different risks. A construction loan expects no income for a while and is repaid by another loan later. A term loan expects steady income from day one and is repaid gradually from that income. Using a term loan to fund construction, or an overdraft to fund a building, mismatches the loan to the risk.

The professional framing: the five types

Construction or interim loan

Funds building costs during the build. Drawn in stages as work is certified. Usually interest-only, with interest often paid from a reserve inside the loan itself. Repaid by a take-out loan or by conversion once the building is complete and stabilised. Priced higher than a term loan because completion and lease-up risks are still open.

Term or permanent mortgage

Funds a stabilised, income-producing building. Repaid from net operating income through regular payments of principal and interest, called amortisation. Carries a coverage covenant tested over the life of the loan. Priced lower because the main risks have been removed.

Construction-to-permanent facility

Combines both in one agreement. It converts automatically from a construction loan to a term loan once agreed conditions are met, such as practical completion and a coverage ratio held for a set number of months. The advantage is certainty: you know the take-out before you start. The cost is that the bank must underwrite both stages at once, so terms can be tighter.

Bridge loan

Funds a short gap, for example between completion and a sale, or between acquisition and a refinance. Short term, higher rate, and repaid by a specific identified event. A bridge without a credible exit is not a bridge; it is a problem with a deadline.

Corporate loan or overdraft

Funds working capital for a business: payroll, inventory, timing gaps. Repaid from the business's general cash flow and usually repayable on demand. Not suitable to fund a building, because a demand facility can be withdrawn just as your project needs it most.

The professional framing: recourse and the borrower

Two further words describe any loan. The first is the borrower. Development loans are usually made to a single-purpose company that owns only the project, so its assets and liabilities are kept separate from the sponsor's other affairs. The second is recourse. A non-recourse loan can be repaid only from the project and its security; a full-recourse loan lets the lender pursue the sponsor personally through a guarantee. Construction loans to smaller or first-time sponsors are often partly or fully recourse, while term loans on stabilised buildings are more often limited recourse. These are commercial practices that vary by market and lender [unverified — confirm with each lender]. Week 4 returns to guarantees in detail, because recourse is where a financing becomes personal.

A worked example

A hypothetical US$4,000,000 project uses three facilities in sequence.

  1. Land purchase. The sponsor buys land for US$600,000 using equity. No loan, because a bank will rarely lend against bare land with no approvals.
  2. Construction. A construction loan of US$2,600,000, 65 percent of cost, drawn monthly over 18 months, interest-only at 9 percent. Average drawn balance is about half the loan, so interest during the build is roughly US$1,300,000 times 9 percent times 1.5 years, which is about US$175,500. This interest is included in the project cost and funded by an interest reserve.
  3. Take-out. On stabilisation, a term mortgage at 7 percent over 25 years repays the construction loan. Payments include principal, so the loan falls over time.

If instead the sponsor had funded construction from a US$2,600,000 overdraft, the bank could have called it at month 12 with the building half finished. The rate might have been similar; the risk was entirely different.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the take-out. A construction loan is designed to be repaid by someone else. If rates rise, the market weakens or the building leases slowly, the take-out lender may offer less than the construction loan balance, leaving a gap you must fund. This is called refinancing risk, and it is why lenders and sponsors alike prefer a committed take-out or a construction-to-permanent facility where available.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner looks only at the interest rate when comparing facilities. A lower-rate facility with a short maturity, an on-demand clause or no conversion right can be far more dangerous than a higher-rate one that is committed through stabilisation. Compare the rate, the term, how the loan is repaid, and what happens if the exit is late.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, draw the project as a timeline with three bars: land and pre-development, construction, and stabilised operation. Write the facility type that suits each bar, and the event that repays it. Then ask of each facility: what repays this, when, and what if that event is six months late? Where the answer is weak, look for a committed take-out, a conversion option or a longer construction term with an extension right. Professional sign-off required: lawyer for the loan agreement, especially conversion conditions and on-demand clauses.

A useful parallel from operations: a facility is like a shift handover. The construction loan must hand over cleanly to the term loan, with conditions both sides agreed in advance. A handover negotiated at the last minute is where incidents happen.
checklist: Construction loan: staged draws, interest-only, repaid by take-out or conversion.
Term mortgage: funds a stabilised building, amortises from net operating income, carries a coverage covenant.
Construction-to-permanent: one facility that converts when conditions are met.
Bridge: short, expensive, and only as good as its identified exit.
Overdraft or corporate loan: working capital, often on demand, not for buildings.
Compare term, repayment source and exit risk, not only the rate.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A lender offers a 12-month construction loan at a low rate for a project with an 18-month build and no committed take-out. What is wrong, and what would you ask for?
selftest.a: The maturity is shorter than the build, so the loan falls due before the building is finished, let alone stabilised, and there is no committed repayment source. Ask for a term covering construction plus a realistic lease-up period, an extension option on defined conditions, and ideally a construction-to-permanent structure or a committed take-out.

title: The construction-loan lifecycle, from commitment to conversion
summary: A construction loan is paid out in stages against independently certified progress, with your equity spent first, retention held back and a cost-to-complete test at every draw. Once the building is complete and leased, it converts or is repaid.
body:
A construction loan is never handed over as a lump sum; it is released in monthly draws against work an independent professional has certified. Mr Shabazz, the in-balance test at every draw is the clause that catches most developers, so learn it before you sign anything.

In plain English

Once a bank approves a construction loan, the money still sits with the bank. You earn access to it in stages. First you satisfy a list of conditions. Then you spend your own equity. Then, each month, the contractor bills, an independent cost professional confirms the work is done, and the bank pays. At the end, the loan is repaid or turned into a long-term mortgage.

The professional framing: the lifecycle step by step

  1. Commitment letter signed. The approved terms and the conditions precedent, called CPs.
  2. CPs satisfied. Title registered, security signed and registered, insurance assigned to the bank, approvals and the construction contract delivered, legal opinions issued.
  3. Equity in first. Most lenders require your full equity to be spent before their first draw. Some allow equity and loan to be spent in proportion, called pro rata; that is a valuable concession to negotiate.
  4. Monthly draws. The contractor submits a payment application; the bank's monitoring quantity surveyor or cost consultant inspects and certifies work done; the bank pays the certified amount, often directly to the contractor.
  5. Retention. A percentage of each certified payment is held back until defects are fixed after completion. The percentage is set in the contract [unverified — common practice varies by market].
  6. Cost-to-complete test. At every draw the bank checks that the undrawn loan plus any remaining equity still covers the full cost to finish. If not, you must fund the gap before the next draw. This is the in-balance requirement.
  7. Practical completion. Occupancy permits, the final cost certificate and an as-built appraisal.
  8. Stabilisation and conversion. Once the building meets the bank's income test, for example a coverage ratio held for a set number of months, the loan converts to an amortising term loan or another lender repays it.

The professional framing: monitoring discipline

Expect the lender to require regular progress reports, expenditure statements and site inspections throughout the build. Lenders typically expect at least monthly reporting on a commercial construction facility [unverified — confirm with each lender]. Treat this as a feature: a reporting rhythm forces early detection of overruns, exactly as a daily site report does.

The professional framing: who is paid, and how

Many lenders pay certified amounts directly to the contractor rather than to the borrower, so the bank knows its money went into the building. Some also require lien waivers or statutory declarations from the contractor and major subcontractors at each draw, confirming they have been paid for earlier work, because an unpaid subcontractor can register a claim against the property that ranks awkwardly against the bank. Draw timing matters too. If certification takes two weeks and payment another week, your contractor waits three weeks or more after month end, and will price that wait into the contract. Agree the certification and payment timeline in writing before signing the construction contract, and align the contract's payment terms with the bank's draw cycle so you are not caught between them.

A worked example

A hypothetical project costs US$3,000,000, including a US$150,000 contingency and a US$180,000 interest reserve. The loan is US$1,950,000, 65 percent of cost. Equity is US$1,050,000.

  1. Months 1 to 6: the sponsor spends the full US$1,050,000 of equity on land, design, approvals and early works. The bank has lent nothing.
  2. Month 7: first draw. The cost consultant certifies US$200,000 of work. Retention of 10 percent, US$20,000, is held back. The bank pays US$180,000 to the contractor.
  3. Month 12: the bank runs the cost-to-complete test. Spent to date: US$1,050,000 equity plus US$900,000 of loan, so US$1,950,000. Revised cost to finish, after a foundation problem: US$1,250,000. Undrawn loan: US$1,950,000 minus US$900,000, which is US$1,050,000.
  4. The test fails by US$1,250,000 minus US$1,050,000, which is US$200,000. The project is out of balance.
  5. The bank stops further draws until the sponsor deposits US$200,000. Until then, the contractor is not paid and may slow or stop work.

The contingency had already been used by month 10. The sponsor needed liquid money outside the project, and needed it within days, not months.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is running out of money mid-build because the in-balance test fails and you have no reserve to fund the gap. The test is automatic and unsentimental. A sponsor who has put every available dollar into the initial equity has nothing left when the test bites. That is why lenders look for liquidity outside the project, and why your own planning should hold a reserve beyond the contingency.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets that construction interest is a cost. Interest accrues on drawn balances throughout the build and must be budgeted, usually as an interest reserve funded by the loan itself. Leaving it out understates total cost, which overstates the bank's share, which causes the cost-to-complete test to fail later. Also budget for the bank's own costs: its legal fees, its cost consultant, its appraisal and its arrangement fee are almost always charged to you.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build a draw schedule month by month before you apply: equity spend, loan draws, retention held, interest accrued and the cost-to-complete position at each month. Run it again with a 15 percent overrun and ask where the shortfall money would come from and how fast. Negotiate for pro rata equity, a clear certification timeline and a defined cure period for an out-of-balance finding. Professional sign-off required: licensed cost consultant or quantity surveyor for the budget and draw certifications; lawyer for the draw and in-balance clauses.
checklist: Conditions precedent must be satisfied before any draw.
Equity usually goes in first; negotiate pro rata where possible.
Each draw is certified by an independent cost professional before payment.
Retention is held back from each certified payment until defects are fixed.
The cost-to-complete test can stop draws until you fund any gap.
Budget construction interest and the lender's own costs into total project cost.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: At month 14 of an 18-month build, the bank's cost consultant says the remaining cost is US$900,000 and the undrawn loan is US$750,000. Your contingency is used up. What happens, and what should you have done earlier?
selftest.a: The project is out of balance by US$150,000. The bank will stop draws until you deposit that amount, and the contractor may slow or stop. Earlier, you should have held a liquid reserve outside the project for exactly this, tracked cost-to-complete monthly yourself so the gap was seen early, negotiated a cure period, and held a contingency an independent cost consultant considered adequate.

apply: Build a six-month draw schedule for a hypothetical US$1,000,000 project with a 65 percent loan, showing equity, draws, 10 percent retention and the cost-to-complete position each month.

title: Week 2 review: construction risk and the loan lifecycle
summary: Six questions on the four construction risks, what tips a lender to yes, loan types and how a construction loan is paid out. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.
body:
This week moved from the bank to the building: the four risks, the factors that tip a yes, the right facility for each stage, and how draws really work. Mr Shabazz, answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

Question 1. Name the four risks a construction lender prices and the strongest evidence that closes each.

Answer. Completion: a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum contract with a capable contractor, an independent budget and contingency, and permits. Lease-up: signed pre-leases or pre-sales, supported by a market study and rent comparisons. Cash flow: a coverage ratio comfortably above the minimum under stress. Exit: clean registered title, a realistic appraisal, insurance and enforceable security. The risks dominate in time order, and completion is usually the one that matters most because a half-built building is worth very little.

Question 2. Which factor usually carries the most weight in tipping a lender to yes, and why?

Answer. Your own cash, spent first and ranking behind the bank. It absorbs the first losses, so the bank's position is protected, and it proves conviction, because a sponsor with real money at risk behaves carefully. After it, in rough order of weight, come cost certainty, income certainty, a clean legal position, coverage headroom, sponsor depth, simplicity and relationship value. Weights vary by lender and should be confirmed with each.

Question 3. How does a first-time developer answer "who has done this before"?

Answer. By renting a track record: an experienced contractor on a fixed or guaranteed-maximum price, an independent cost consultant, a development manager or owner's representative with completed buildings, a professional property manager and recognised advisers. She names them and their projects in the package, and keeps her own assumptions conservative, because inexperience combined with optimism reads as double risk.

Question 4. Why is an overdraft or demand facility unsuitable to fund a building?

Answer. Because it can usually be called on demand and is repaid from general business cash flow, while a building needs committed money for a fixed build period and is repaid later by income or a take-out loan. The lender could withdraw it mid-build, exactly when the project is most vulnerable. Construction needs a construction or construction-to-permanent facility with a term covering the build and lease-up.

Question 5. What is a cost-to-complete or in-balance test, and what happens when a project fails it?

Answer. At each draw the bank checks that the undrawn loan plus any remaining equity covers the full cost to finish. If the cost to finish is larger, the project is out of balance and the bank stops draws until the sponsor funds the gap, usually from liquid money outside the project. The contractor may slow or stop meanwhile. The defence is an adequate contingency, a separate liquid reserve, monthly cost-to-complete tracking and a negotiated cure period.

Question 6. Calculation. A construction loan of US$2,000,000 is drawn evenly over 20 months at 9 percent a year, interest-only. Roughly how much interest accrues during the build, and where should it appear?

Answer. With even draws, the average drawn balance is about half the loan, US$1,000,000. Interest is roughly US$1,000,000 times 9 percent times 20 over 12 years, which is US$150,000. It belongs in the total project cost, usually funded by an interest reserve inside the loan. Leaving it out understates cost and causes the in-balance test to fail later.

Recap

A construction lender is betting on a sequence of future events, and reduces that bet to four risks. Your package is the evidence that closes each one before you apply, because banks lend against risk already removed. The most persuasive evidence is your own cash spent first, followed by fixed costs and signed income. A new sponsor compensates for inexperience with a hired team and conservative assumptions, not with optimism.

Each stage of a project needs the right facility: construction or construction-to-permanent during the build, a term loan once stabilised, a bridge only with a firm exit, and never a demand facility for a building. Once a construction loan is approved, money flows in certified monthly draws, with retention held back and the in-balance test run at every draw. Construction interest and the lender's own costs are part of total cost.

One more connection is worth making explicit. Every condition in a lender's offer is the price of a risk left open. A required pre-lease percentage prices lease-up risk; an overrun guarantee prices completion risk; a lower loan-to-cost ratio prices both. When you read an offer, translate each condition back into the risk it covers, and ask whether closing that risk yourself, for example by signing a guaranteed-maximum contract or a pre-lease, would cost less than accepting the condition. Very often it does, and the lender will happily remove a condition once the underlying risk is gone.

Finally, remember that recourse turns a project loan into a personal one. A construction loan to a new sponsor is often backed by a guarantee, so the in-balance test is not only the project's problem; it is a call on your own liquidity. Plan your outside reserves with that in mind, and keep them genuinely liquid rather than tied up in other property.

Mr Shabazz, the habit to carry forward is the draw schedule. A month-by-month table of equity, draws, retention, interest and cost-to-complete is the single most useful tool you can bring to a construction lender, and running it again with a 15 percent overrun shows you, before the bank does, how much liquidity you need to keep outside the project. Next week turns to the numbers that size a loan: net operating income, loan-to-cost, loan-to-value, coverage and debt yield, and how to find which one binds.
checklist: Four risks: completion, lease-up, cash flow, exit.
Your cash in first carries the most weight with a lender.
First-time sponsors rent a track record and keep assumptions conservative.
Match the facility to the stage; never fund a building with a demand facility.
The in-balance test stops draws until you fund any gap.
Construction interest, at roughly half the loan times the rate times the build period, belongs in cost.

selftest.q: Your contractor tells you mid-build that a design change will add US$120,000. Your contingency has US$40,000 left. Walk through what the lender's process will do and what you must prepare.
selftest.a: The cost consultant will add the change to the cost to complete. With only US$40,000 of contingency left, the project will likely be out of balance by about US$80,000 at the next draw test, so the bank will stop draws until you fund it. Prepare by notifying the lender early, getting the change priced and certified, and having liquid funds ready to deposit; consider whether the change can be deferred or value-engineered.
